title: Move Semantics and Rvalue References
relevance: Tests whether candidates can explain C++11 value categories, avoid wasteful copies of temporaries, and correctly transfer ownership of resources in production C++.

phases.goal: Establish lvalue vs rvalue categories and how T& versus T&& bind.

must_hit.point: An lvalue refers to a persistent memory location with a name or identifiable address; an rvalue is a temporary that does not persist beyond the expression that uses it.
must_hit.evidence_hint: Candidate contrasts named objects like x with temporaries/literals, and notes you cannot assign to an rvalue.

must_hit.point: C++11 rvalue references (T&&) bind only to rvalues; ordinary lvalue references (T&) bind only to lvalues, while const T& can also bind to temporaries.
must_hit.evidence_hint: Candidate walks binding rules: T& to named lvalue OK, T& to temporary error; T&& to temporary OK, T&& to named lvalue error.

must_hit.point: Binding an rvalue reference to a temporary gives exclusive access, so you may safely modify it or strip its resources.
must_hit.evidence_hint: Candidate says the temporary is about to be destroyed and no other code retains usable access to it.

probes: What is the difference between an lvalue and an rvalue, and what can T&& bind to that T& cannot?

hints.1: Think about whether the expression names a lasting object or is only a temporary.
hints.2: Compare binding of T&, const T&, and T&& to named variables versus literals/temporaries.
hints.3: Lvalues persist and bind to T&; rvalues are temporaries and T&& exists to bind only to them, giving exclusive access.

phases.goal: Establish how move construction/assignment steal resources and how std::move and special-member rules enable that.

must_hit.point: A move constructor/assignment steals pointers and handles from the source, then immediately nulls the source so its destructor will not free the stolen resources; the source is left in a valid but unspecified state.
must_hit.evidence_hint: Candidate describes pointer steal, nulling data/size, and that delete[] on nullptr in the destructor is safe.

must_hit.point: std::move does not move; it is an unconditional cast to an rvalue reference so a named lvalue becomes eligible to be moved from.
must_hit.evidence_hint: Candidate says std::move(s1) forces the move constructor path and that s1 should not be used afterward except to assign to or destroy.

must_hit.point: Declaring a custom destructor, copy constructor, or copy assignment suppresses implicit generation of move operations, so the class falls back to copying unless moves are explicitly defaulted or defined.
must_hit.evidence_hint: Candidate recalls that a user-declared destructor alone can suppress moves, and that = default on moves restores them.

must_hit.point: The Rule of 3 says defining any of destructor/copy ctor/copy assignment usually requires all three; the Rule of 5 adds move constructor and move assignment for performance; the Rule of 0 prefers owning no raw resources so the compiler generates all five correctly.
must_hit.evidence_hint: Candidate lists Rules of 0/3/5 and ties Rule of 0 to std::string, std::vector, or std::unique_ptr.

probes: Walk through implementing a move constructor for a class that owns a heap buffer, and say what std::move actually does.

hints.1: Compare photocopying a temporary's buffer with taking its pointer.
hints.2: Cover steal-then-null, valid-but-unspecified state, and the cast nature of std::move.
hints.3: Move ctor takes T&& noexcept, copies size/data then zeros the source; std::move only casts to T&& so the move overload is selected.

phases.goal: Contrast deep-copying temporaries with moving, and RVO with forcing a move.

must_hit.point: Without move semantics, initializing from a returned temporary forces a deep copy of owned heap data and then destroys the temporary's copy, which is wasteful for large buffers.
must_hit.evidence_hint: Candidate describes allocate-and-copy of the returned IntArray-style buffer followed by delete of the temporary's identical buffer.

must_hit.point: Copy elision / RVO can construct a returned local directly into the caller's object so neither copy nor move occurs; writing return std::move(local) prevents RVO and forces a move.
must_hit.evidence_hint: Candidate prefers bare return local; and warns that return std::move(local); blocks RVO.

must_hit.point: Prefer Rule of 0 resource wrappers over hand-written Rule of 5 special members when possible, because the compiler then generates correct copy and move operations.
must_hit.evidence_hint: Candidate argues for std::string/vector/unique_ptr ownership instead of managing raw new/delete by hand.

probes: When returning a large object by value, when is a move better than a copy, and when is even a move worse than doing nothing?

hints.1: Think about what happens to a temporary's heap buffer after a deep copy.
hints.2: Separate pre-move deep copy cost from RVO, where the local is built in place.
hints.3: Move beats copying temporaries by stealing pointers; RVO is better still, and return std::move(local) can disable it.

phases.goal: Apply moves in templates and library contexts: perfect forwarding and noexcept moves.

must_hit.point: In a deduced template parameter, T&& is a forwarding/universal reference that can bind to both lvalues and rvalues via reference collapsing (& & / & && / && & -> &; && && -> &&).
must_hit.evidence_hint: Candidate explains that an lvalue of type int deduces T as int& so the parameter collapses to an lvalue reference.

must_hit.point: std::forward<T> is a conditional cast that turns the argument into an rvalue only if the original argument was an rvalue, preserving value category through wrappers.
must_hit.evidence_hint: Candidate contrasts unconditional std::move with std::forward that restores the caller's lvalue/rvalue category to the overload set.

must_hit.point: Move constructors should be noexcept because containers such as std::vector only move on reallocation when the move cannot throw; otherwise they fall back to copying to keep the strong exception guarantee.
must_hit.evidence_hint: Candidate ties noexcept on moves to vector buffer reallocation choosing move versus safe copy.

probes: What does std::move actually do, why should a move constructor be noexcept, and how does std::forward differ from std::move in a forwarding reference wrapper?

hints.1: Recall the interview points on std::move and noexcept moves with std::vector.
hints.2: Distinguish unconditional cast versus conditional cast, and mention reference collapsing for T&&.
hints.3: std::move always yields T&&; std::forward<T> preserves category; vector reallocates with move only if the move is noexcept.

tradeoffs.topic: Deep copy of a temporary vs move
tradeoffs.strong_answer: Copying a returned owning object allocates and duplicates the heap buffer then destroys the temporary's buffer; a move steals the pointer/handles and nulls the source, avoiding that work.

If you manage raw resources you need the Rule of 3 for safety and the Rule of 5 for efficient moves; prefer Rule of 0 with standard owning types so the compiler generates all five special members correctly.
RVO can elide both copy and move by constructing directly in the caller; return std::move(local) prevents RVO and forces a move constructor call, so prefer return local;
std::move unconditionally casts to an rvalue reference; std::forward<T> conditionally casts to an rvalue only when the original argument was an rvalue, which is required for perfect forwarding.

gotchas.correction: std::move only unconditionally casts to an rvalue reference; the selected move constructor or move assignment does the steal.

gotchas.trap: Writing return std::move(local); to “help” the compiler.
gotchas.correction: That can prevent RVO/copy elision and force a move; return the local by name instead.

gotchas.trap: Declaring a custom destructor (or copy operations) and assuming moves still happen automatically.
gotchas.correction: Those declarations suppress implicit move generation, so returns by value may copy unless moves are explicitly defaulted or defined.

gotchas.trap: Continuing to read a moved-from object as if it still held its old value.
gotchas.correction: After a move the source is valid but unspecified (often empty for std::string); only assign to it or destroy it.

gotchas.trap: Omitting noexcept on a move constructor used with standard containers.
gotchas.correction: std::vector keeps the strong exception guarantee and will copy instead of move on reallocation if the move might throw.
